profile.campus: Prime Dallas, TX campus (DFW01-01, operational/leased, and DFW01-02, under construction, 20 MW / 213,000 sqft combined per Prime own site)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading: This OpenStreetMap record, also named Prime DFW01-01 and carrying the same 1515 Round Table Drive address in Dallas, Texas, as a second, separately-geometried way in this dataset, sits roughly 100 to 150 meters from its identically-named companion, both mapped in the same December 2025 changeset by the same contributor. Prime own Dallas locations page describes DFW01-01 as a single building of 107,000 square feet and 8 megawatts of capacity, part of a two-building campus alongside the under-construction DFW01-02 building at 1455 Round Table Drive, which together are planned to reach 20 megawatts and 213,000 square feet. Because Prime own materials describe only one DFW01-01 building rather than two, this record and its companion most plausibly represent a mapping artifact, such as a duplicated or split campus footprint captured by the same volunteer OpenStreetMap edit, rather than two genuinely distinct leasable structures, though that could not be confirmed with certainty this session absent aerial or field verification. A January 2026 Prime press release confirms DFW01-01 operational status by name, reporting that the facility earned ENERGY STAR certification for superior energy performance alongside a Prime facility in Sacramento. No tenant is named for DFW01-01 in any source reviewed. Prime Data Centers was founded in 2017 in California and is now headquartered at 400 North Ervay Street in Dallas, Texas, describing itself as majority founder-owned and led by founder and CEO Nicholas Laag, with an overall footprint of 28 data centers across 13 campuses and a pipeline exceeding 4 gigawatts spanning Austin, Chicago, Dallas, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Sacramento, Silicon Valley, Frankfurt, Madrid, and a newly announced site in Esbjerg, Denmark. Dallas has grown into one of the largest data center markets in the country over the past decade, driven by relatively low power costs, available land, and a central US location favorable for network latency, factors consistent with Prime decision to headquarter itself in the city while also building an operating campus there.
profile.campus_note: One of 2 buildings OpenStreetMap contributors have mapped under this name in this locality, numbered west to east.

reading.body:
Prime DFW01-01 in Dallas publishes 20 MW of IT capacity, making it the sixth-largest disclosed facility in Texas among 133 mapped sites, though only 13 publish capacity figures.

The facility's 213,000 square feet yields roughly 94 watts per square foot at stated IT load, a power density consistent with mixed-use colocation rather than purpose-built AI training infrastructure. At 40 kW per rack, common for AI training workloads, 20 MW supports approximately 500 racks. At 10 kW per rack, typical of enterprise and GPU colocation mixing, it supports roughly 2,000 racks. The operator has not specified which density the facility targets, so these figures represent bounds on possible capacity rather than confirmed specifications. This ambiguity matters because the same megawatt budget constrains very different workload profiles depending on the facility's actual design.

The facility holds SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001 certifications, qualifying it for enterprise tenants with compliance and security obligations, but publishes no tenant names or workload types. These credentials enable the facility to host regulated workloads but do not indicate whether it is currently used for AI infrastructure, general cloud compute, or enterprise services.

Texas's 133 mapped facilities publish only 389 MW of capacity across 13 of them. Prime DFW01-01 represents 5 percent of that disclosed total. The remaining 120 facilities publish no capacity figures, meaning the true state total is unknown and likely substantially higher than 389 MW. Statewide visibility into grid impact is therefore incomplete.
